# Misreadings {#sec-misreadings}

The book makes one claim: grid type is relative to a frame. Some readings
of it miss that claim, and some readers reach past the book for an
authority that seems to settle the matter first. This appendix collects
those responses as they turn up, with a short answer to each. It will grow.

## "Wikipedia already defines a regular grid" {#sec-mis-wikipedia}

It does, and its definitions agree with this book. They just leave the
frame unstated, because they assume one.

The Wikipedia article *Regular grid* (read 15 October 2026) defines a
regular grid as a tessellation of *n*-dimensional Euclidean space by
congruent parallelotopes. A rectilinear grid is a tessellation by rectangles
or boxes that are not all congruent. A curvilinear grid has the same
combinatorial structure as a regular grid but quadrilateral cells instead
of rectangles. Every one of these is a statement about the shape of cells
*in a space*, and the space is fixed in advance: Euclidean, with Cartesian
coordinates. The article never mentions geographic coordinates, map
projections or coordinate reference systems.

Earth data does not come with a single Euclidean space. Longitude and
latitude are not Euclidean coordinates, and each map projection supplies a
different plane. Applied to Earth data, the article's definitions give
different answers depending on which plane you draw the cells in. The
NSIDC 25 km grid is a tessellation by congruent squares in EPSG:3412, which
makes it regular by Wikipedia's definition. Drawn in longitude and latitude,
the same cells are general quadrilaterals, which makes it curvilinear by the
same article's definition (@sec-case-cryosat). Wikipedia does not decide
between those answers. It cannot, because it never asks which plane.

The article's own example of a rectilinear grid makes the point. Its
example is logarithmic graph paper. The lines on log paper are unevenly
spaced in *x* and evenly spaced in log(*x*), so the paper is rectilinear in
one frame and regular in another. That is the claim of this book, in the
article's own example.

**Better authorities.** The article has two references: a MathWorld entry
and Thompson, Soni and Weatherill's *Handbook of Grid Generation*. The
grid-generation literature the handbook represents defines a structured
grid as a mapping. The grid is uniform in a computational (index) space,
and a coordinate transformation carries it into the physical space where it
may be curvilinear. Grid type is a property of that mapping and the space it
lands in, not of the cells alone. The sources this book already relies on
take the same view:

- Balaji's grid standard calls the first three rungs *logically
  rectangular*: "The coordinate space may continue to be physically
  curvilinear; yet, in index space, grid cells will be rectilinear boxes."
  (@sec-two-questions)
- ESMF classifies uniform, rectilinear and curvilinear grids as subtypes of
  logically rectangular grids, with the coordinates stored separately from
  the index structure.
- The CF conventions let one dataset carry native 1D projected or rotated
  coordinates alongside 2D longitude and latitude, tied together by a
  `grid_mapping` variable. CF thereby records that one grid can be 1D and
  regular in one frame and 2D in another (@sec-case-cordex).

So the disagreement is not with Wikipedia. It is with reading a definition
written for one Euclidean space as if it settled a question about
several frames.

## "This is just arguing about words"

The words matter because software and file formats act on them. Treating a
regular grid as curvilinear makes files many thousands of times larger than
they need to be (@sec-costumes). It also replaces exact coordinates with
float32 noise, makes readers refuse or warp grids that need nothing done
(@sec-software), and leads to resampling data that was already on a regular
grid (@sec-problem). None of those costs depends on vocabulary. They all
follow from not asking which frame.

## "So 2D longitude and latitude arrays are wrong"

No. For a genuinely curvilinear grid, such as the NEMO ORCA tripolar grid
(@sec-case-orca) or a satellite swath (@sec-case-viirs), the arrays *are*
the grid, and nothing smaller describes it. Storing longitude and latitude
next to a regular grid's native coordinates is also fine, and CF encourages
it. The trouble starts when the 2D arrays are the only thing stored and the
frame that made the grid regular is lost.

## "A longitude and latitude grid is curvilinear because the Earth is curved"

A grid with uniform steps in longitude and latitude is regular in the
longitude and latitude frame. Its cells shrink toward the poles on the
ground, and its lines are curves when drawn in most projections, but that is
the frame doing its work, not the grid changing type. The curvature of the
Earth is a separate question about the surface the frame sits on. That
question is about wrapping, poles and area, and @sec-edges takes it up.

## "Regular means the cells are all the same size"

Only in the frame. A regular longitude and latitude grid has cells whose
ground area varies with the cosine of latitude, so a 1 degree cell at 80
degrees covers less than a fifth of the area of one at the equator. In the
other direction, NASA's L3 bin scheme has cells of nearly equal area and is
not regular in any frame; it is not even indexed by row and column
(@sec-l3bin). Equal area is a property of cells on the Earth. Regularity is
a property of positions in a frame.
